meta.title: Tamil A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Tamil → English (see the Tamil, recall the meaning) and English → Tamil (see an English meaning, recall the Tamil). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for learners of Tamil, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 264 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days of the week, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words and postpositions every sentence is built out of — and the other 236 are the commonest remaining words of Tamil, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. WHICH TAMIL: the written standard. Tamil is diglossic — people speak a colloquial Tamil that differs from the written language in its verb endings and many common words (written போகிறேன் pōkiṟēṉ, 'I go', is said pōṟēṉ) — and the dictionary forms taught here are the written ones, which every reader of signs, books and news needs and from which the spoken forms can be learnt. Every headword is printed in Tamil script with a romanisation beneath it, Wiktionary's own (ā ī ū ē ō for the long vowels, ṭ ṇ ḷ ḻ for the retroflex sounds, ṉ and ṟ for the alveolar n and r: vīṭu, pōkiṟēṉ), so the deck can be studied before the script is fluent; the Tamil Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the script itself. A verb is shown, as dictionaries show it, by its stem, which is also its plain command (போ, 'go!'). The 239 nouns show their plural and the stem their cases are built on (வீடு, வீட்டை, வீட்டில் — house, the house, in the house); the 96 verbs show their past, where Tamil verbs are irregular, their infinitive and their 'having done' form, and behind the All forms fold their present, past and future by person. Real example sentences come with only 179 of the 500 words — Tatoeba, the open sentence collection, holds just a few hundred translated Tamil sentences — with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
